name: Szent István Park and the Wallenberg Memorial
address: Szent István park, Újlipótváros riverside, Budapest XIII (between Újpesti rakpart and Hollán Ernő utca)
intro: Szent István park is a riverside park in Újlipótváros, in Budapest’s thirteenth district, looking across the Danube towards Margaret Island. It was laid out in the 1930s to designs by Béla Rerrich on the site of a former parquet factory. Among its memorials is a statue of Saint George raised in honour of Raoul Wallenberg.
about: Szent István park lies at the western end of Csanády utca, between Újpesti rakpart and Hollán Ernő utca, on the Danube side of Újlipótváros. It is named after King Stephen I of Hungary and overlooks the river and Margaret Island. The district’s own introduction records that the park came into being on the site of a former parquet factory.

A fountain stands in the middle of the park, and Hungarian Wikipedia lists ping-pong tables, a sports ground and two playgrounds among its facilities. Several statues and memorials stand in the park and on the walls of nearby houses, among them memorials to Raoul Wallenberg and to Ferenc Fejtő. The Wallenberg memorial is a sculpture of Saint George fighting a serpent, which a Wallenberg tribute website describes as a symbol of his fight against the Nazis. Its story is told below.

The park gives the neighbourhood a green edge. The 1928 decree that created it also required the surrounding houses to follow a uniform style, and the streets around the park are lined with five- and six-storey modern apartment buildings. The Dunapark Kávéház, a café at the corner of Pozsonyi út and the park, opened in 1938.

Newer green spaces have since been added nearby to relieve pressure on the park, among them Duna terasz, Ruttkai Éva park, Thurzó park and Gabriel García Márquez park. A city participation process in 2022 proposed refurbished ping-pong and basketball facilities, a ball court, and the opening of a previously closed green area on the northern side, so details of the layout may change. Check the district or city pages for the current state of the park.
tips: Walk to the riverside edge of the park for the view across the Danube to Margaret Island, then continue to the island itself, which has its own page on this site.

Look for the Saint George sculpture and the other memorials; some stand on the walls of houses around the park rather than inside it. Treat the Wallenberg memorial as the place of remembrance that it is, and be considerate when photographing, since this is also a local neighbourhood park.
The Dunapark Kávéház at the corner of Pozsonyi út and the park has been a neighbourhood landmark since 1938; check its current status before planning a stop.
Because refurbishment of the park was proposed in a 2022 city consultation, look at the district or city websites for any works, fenced areas or changes to the park before you go.
Pozsonyi út and the streets around the park are lined with the 1930s apartment blocks that the 1928 decree called for, and they make an easy walk with the park as the starting point.

history.intro: The park is a product of interwar city planning, and its best-known monument has a history of removal and return.

sections.heading: A park on the parquet factory site
paragraphs: A 1928 decree of the Fővárosi Közmunkák Tanácsa, the capital’s public works council, decided to create the park on the site of a former parquet factory. It was laid out in 1934–1935 to designs by the architect Béla Rerrich. At first it was called Lipótvárosi park, then Rakovszky park after its initiator Iván Rakovszky, and it has carried the name Szent István since 1937.

The park was rebuilt in 1961 to plans by Vilmos Jancsó and again in 1974 to plans by Veronika Csorba. The last major renovation, in 1997–1998, renewed the paths, planting, furniture and playgrounds. A rose garden was planted by the city’s park company, Főkert, in 2010.

sections.heading: Raoul Wallenberg and the Saint George statue
paragraphs: Raoul Wallenberg, a Swedish diplomat, reached the Swedish legation in Budapest on 9 July 1944. With colleagues he issued protective passports and rented 32 buildings that he declared extraterritorial; English Wikipedia says they eventually housed almost 10,000 people. He was called to Soviet headquarters in Debrecen on 17 January 1945 and disappeared that day. Raoul Wallenberg utca in the thirteenth district has carried his name since 1945, and the district is where the so-called Swedish houses stood in 1944–1945.

According to the Wallenberg tribute website, the sculptor Pál Pátzay made a statue of Saint George fighting a serpent in Wallenberg’s honour, dated 10 April 1949, for this park. It was removed before it could be unveiled and now stands in Debrecen. A full-size replica based on Pátzay’s work, made by Sándor Győrfi, was set up in the original place on 18 April 1999 at the initiative of the Wallenberg Statue Committee. Hungarian Wikipedia’s article on the park mentions the Wallenberg memorial but gives no date or sculptor, so these details rest on the tribute website alone.

name: Erzsébet Square and the Danubius Fountain
address: Erzsébet tér, Budapest V (between Bajcsy-Zsilinszky út and Bécsi utca)
intro: Erzsébet tér is a green square in the middle of Pest’s Inner City, between Bajcsy-Zsilinszky út and Bécsi utca. Its centrepiece is the neo-Renaissance Danubius Fountain, designed by Miklós Ybl and Béla Brestyánszky and built in 1880–1883, which the heritage register says was moved here from Kálvin tér in 1957–1958.
about: Erzsébet tér is a public square and park in District V, in the centre of Pest. Over the years it has been a cemetery, a market, a garden and a bus station site. At its centre stands the Danubius Fountain, which is a listed monument.

The heritage register describes the fountain as a freestanding, three-lobed, multi-tiered structure. The lower basin has six lobes and rests on steps, and a triangular base rises from its centre. Allegorical female figures at the corners personify three Hungarian rivers, the Tisza, the Dráva and the Száva, with wall basins decorated with masks and shells between them. A smaller circular basin sits at the top, crowned by a figure of Danubius standing on a dolphin.

Around the fountain stand the former bus station building, designed by István Nyiri and built in 1948–1949, and a large Ferris wheel, which Hungarian Wikipedia says has stood on the square since the summer of 2013. The bus station building has had monument protection since 1977. It housed the Design Terminal in 2011–2016, and a welovebudapest article from 2020 described a renovated playground, a basketball and mini-football court and a skateboarding track elsewhere on the square.

The square is a natural pause on a walk through downtown Pest. Deák tér, Vörösmarty tér and St Stephen’s Basilica all have their own pages on this site, and in 1948 the city council decided to connect Erzsébet tér with Deák Ferenc tér.
tips: Walk all the way round the fountain to find the three river figures and the Danubius figure on the dolphin that the heritage register describes; the masks and shells on the wall basins are easy to miss from a distance.
The former bus station building is a protected monument but its tenants have changed over the years, from the Design Terminal to other uses. Check what is there now before planning around it.
The square makes a good break between the Deák tér area and the Basilica, and Vörösmarty tér is within easy reach; all three have their own pages here.
The heritage register page is a useful reference for the fountain’s details, including the original inscription.
For the Ferris wheel and the venues around the square, use the operators’ own pages for current information rather than relying on older guides.

history.intro: The square’s story runs from a burial ground and market to a public garden, and on to a bus station and a recent park.

sections.heading: From cemetery and market to garden
paragraphs: A welovebudapest history says the site was a cemetery in the seventeenth century and was later turned into a marketplace. Hungarian Wikipedia adds that the area outside the Váci gate of Pest’s city walls was known first as Új tér and later as Vásártér. The same article dates the name Erzsébet tér to 1858, whereas the welovebudapest article places the fencing of the square and its naming after Empress Elisabeth in 1872, so the sources do not agree on the date.

Preparations to turn the site into a park began in 1854, according to welovebudapest, and a Neo-Renaissance kiosk with a café was built there in 1870. In 1907 it was converted into an Art Nouveau building housing the National Salon, which was demolished in 1960. Hungarian Wikipedia says it was demolished after the Second World War, without giving a year.

sections.heading: The Danubius Fountain
paragraphs: The heritage register dates the fountain to 1880–1883 and names Miklós Ybl and Béla Brestyánszky as its architects. It was moved from Kálvin tér to its present site in 1957–1958. The lower basin originally bore a cartouche inscription naming the Pesti Hazai Első Takarékpénztár Egyesület, a savings association, as the donor to the capital, with the years 1880–1883.

Hungarian Wikipedia words the history differently, saying the fountain in the middle of the square replaced an original that stood at Kálvin tér and was destroyed in the Second World War. This page follows the heritage register’s account of a move and does not try to settle the difference.

sections.heading: Bus station, theatre pit and park
paragraphs: A bus station was built on the square in 1948–1949, and the welovebudapest article calls it the country’s largest. Hungarian Wikipedia says its traffic moved to the Népliget bus station when that opened in 2002. In 1998 work began on a National Theatre building on the square, but it stopped the same year for lack of funds, and the pit became the Gödör cultural centre in 2002. The Gödör moved to Király utca in 2012, and the Akvárium Klub became the square’s main nightlife venue.
The park was renovated in 2006.

name: Vérmező and the Hungarian Jacobins' Memorial Stone
address: Vérmező park, Krisztinaváros (western foot of Castle Hill), Budapest I
intro: Vérmező, the Blood Meadow, is a wide park at the western foot of Castle Hill in Krisztinaváros, Budapest’s first district. Its name recalls the execution of Ignác Martinovics and other leaders of the Hungarian Jacobin conspiracy on 20 May 1795. A coffin-shaped memorial stone by Frigyes Matzon, unveiled in 1955, marks the event.
about: Vérmező is a public park in Krisztinaváros, District I, at the western foot of Várhegy, Castle Hill. Hungarian Wikipedia gives its boundaries as Attila út, Krisztina körút and Mikó utca, and says the Ördög-árok stream runs beneath it.

The memorial stone to the Hungarian Jacobins is a coffin-shaped block almost two and a half metres long, the work of Frigyes Matzon. It was unveiled in 1955, on the 160th anniversary of the executions, at the end of the park nearest Széll Kálmán tér. Its inscription names five leaders of the movement: Ignác Martinovics, Ferenc Szentmarjai, József Hajnóczy, János Lackovics and Jakab Sigray. Two further men, Pál Őz and Sándor Szolartsik, are also named on it.

Several other works stand in the park. Hungarian Wikipedia lists a memorial to the Buda Volunteer Regiment from 1967 by István Szabó, István Kiss’s dragonfly composition Szitakötők from 1979 near the Mikó utca playground, a reclining figure from 1984 by István János Nagy, and a statue of the poet Mihály Babits from 2008 by László Marton, which was the first public statue of Babits in Budapest. Babits lived the last ten years of his life in houses beside the park.

The park lies between the Castle District and the streets of Krisztinaváros, and Hungarian Wikipedia describes it as part of a green corridor that carries fresh air from the Buda hills towards the Danube. It is a place where Budapest residents walk, rest and play, so a visit is best treated as part of a stroll rather than a stop in itself.
tips: Look for the memorial stone at the end of the park towards Széll Kálmán tér. It is a coffin-shaped block of stone, so read the inscription to understand what it commemorates.
Treat the stone as a memorial to men who were executed: a short pause is more appropriate than posing for photographs on it.
Combine the park with a walk up Castle Hill; the Buda Castle District has its own page on this site, and the Vienna Gate is within reach.
The Kun Béla memorial that once stood at the northern end of the park was moved to Memento Park in 1991, and Memento Park has its own page on this site.
Check the district municipality’s website for works, events or temporary closures in the park.

history.intro: For centuries the meadow was kept free of buildings below the castle, and in 1795 it became the site of one of Hungary’s best-known political executions.

sections.heading: A military zone below the castle
paragraphs: Hungarian Wikipedia says the area, then a glacis or open firing zone, was declared a military protection zone in 1752, one musket-shot from the walls, and building on it was banned. In 1784 the governing council abolished the glacis and offered free plots to anyone willing to build. The castle used the land as a hayfield, and in the nineteenth century it served as a military training ground. The same article says the meadow took its present form in 1830–1833, when roads were rebuilt and the Ördög-árok stream was vaulted over.
The meadow hosted a Millennium military parade and folk festival in 1896.

sections.heading: The Jacobin executions of 1795
paragraphs: Ignác Martinovics and the other leaders of the Hungarian Jacobin conspiracy were executed here. The Hungarian Wikipedia article and English Wikipedia both give the date as 20 May 1795, and so does the Vérmező section of the First District municipality’s page. That page gives 20 March 1795 elsewhere, in its introduction to Krisztinaváros, so the sources do not fully agree, and this guide uses the date that appears in three places.

The memorial inscription, as the district page reproduces it, names Őz and Szolartsik with a year that is printed as 1975, evidently a typographical slip; this page leaves that detail out. The municipality says the district name Vérmező still recalls the executions.

sections.heading: Rubble, planting and monuments
paragraphs: Hungarian Wikipedia describes the meadow as the last place where light courier aircraft could land during the siege of Budapest. After the war the grassy basin was filled with rubble from Castle Hill, and replanting began in 1948. Antal Csorna designed the southern corner and Antal Jancsó the northern and central parts.

A multi-figure memorial to Béla Kun by Imre Varga was unveiled at the northern end in 1986, dismantled in 1991 and moved to Memento Park. The Matzon stone of 1955 remains the park’s historical marker.

name: Óbuda Island (Hajógyári Island)
address: Óbudai-sziget, Budapest III (reached from Óbuda by the K-bridge)
intro: Budapest’s Óbudai-sziget, better known as Hajógyári-sziget or Shipyard Island, is a Danube island of 108 hectares in Budapest’s third district, reached from Óbuda by the K-bridge. A shipyard worked here for more than a century. Today it is a recreation area and the home of the Sziget Festival every August.
about: Óbuda Island lies in the Danube in Budapest’s third district. Hungarian Wikipedia gives its area as 108 hectares and its length as 2,750 metres, and says it is separated from Óbuda by a branch of the river 70–80 metres wide. The Árpád Bridge crosses its southern end. The island is commonly called Hajógyári-sziget because the famous shipyard once stood at its southern end.

Today most of the island is a recreation park with ornamental shrubs and flowers. The former shipyard buildings now house offices, warehouses and a yacht club, and the Magyar Yacht Klub operates from the island’s harbour. The city’s planning page says dog walking is the island’s main everyday use, and that the park areas belong to the Budapest Capital Municipality, while the built-up southern and western areas belong to the Hungarian State.

The island also has a natural side. Hungarian Wikipedia reports a strip of soft-wood floodplain forest with white willows and black poplars about 200 years old, and says the northern tip is a stopover for migrating waterbirds. It says the capital’s assembly has declared the floodplain forest a locally significant nature reserve. Sources differ on which bank the surviving forest lies along.

In practice a visit depends on timing. The city’s page says the southern area is currently closed to public use and that the plan is to open it and link it by bus. The Sziget Festival brings large crowds in August and can change access to the island, so check the official sites for the current state of the island before travelling.
tips: Walk or cycle over the K-bridge from Óbuda; Hungarian Wikipedia says a bus line, number 226, uses it on weekends in the warmer part of the year, but check the current BKK information before relying on it.
Check the island’s access arrangements around the Sziget Festival in August; the build-up and the festival itself can restrict or change access.
The northern gallery forest and the floodplain woodland are the natural highlights; keep to paths and be considerate of wildlife, which the city plan says it wants to protect.
The southern part of the island is described on the city’s page as currently closed, so do not plan a route there without checking.
Combine the island with Óbuda’s Fő tér and the Aquincum Museum, both of which have their own pages on this site.

history.intro: The island’s history runs from Roman-era traces to a shipyard and then to leisure use.

sections.heading: From sandbar to shipyard
paragraphs: Hungarian Wikipedia describes the island as originally a sandbar made of two nearby parts. The district page for Óbuda says the Romans already used the location, and Hungarian Wikipedia adds that remains of a palace associated with Hadrian were found on the former shipyard site and still await excavation. English Wikipedia says the island was a wooded hunting preserve in the time of King Matthias Corvinus and passed to the Zichy family in the seventeenth century.

The Óbuda district page says the shipyard operated from 1835 to 1991. English Wikipedia credits Count István Széchenyi with establishing the Óbuda shipyard and gives 1836 for the launch of its first ship, the steamboat Árpád. The yard occupied 28 hectares, and the rest of the island was farmland.

sections.heading: Parks and the festival
paragraphs: May the 9th Park was created in 1973, according to English Wikipedia, to mark the centenary of the union of Óbuda, Pest and Buda. The Sziget Festival began in 1993 as Diáksziget, the Students’ Island, and was renamed Sziget Fesztivál in 2002. Hungarian Wikipedia says it has been held on the island every August since 1993.
A large hotel and entertainment complex was planned for the island, but English Wikipedia says the project failed in 2013 and the government bought the land back.

sections.heading: The city’s plan for the island
paragraphs: Since early 2020 the city has run a planning process for the island, with a questionnaire that drew about 1,600 respondents, draft plans and on-site meetings. The strategic plan that came out of it puts protecting natural values and biodiversity first and proposes less parking, better park infrastructure, and opening the southern area. It also includes renovation of the K-bridge and coordination with the festival organisers to reduce the festival’s impact on protected areas.

name: Buda Capuchin Church
intro: The Buda Capuchin Church on Fő utca, beside Corvin tér, is the parish church of Alsóviziváros, dedicated to Saint Elizabeth of Hungary. It stands on the site of an Ottoman mosque, whose façade walls survive in its side walls. Its present Romantic exterior dates from the 1850s, and Capuchin friars serve the parish again today.
about: The Budai kapucinus templom is the parish church of the Alsóvizivárosi Szent Erzsébet parish, dedicated to Saint Elizabeth of Hungary. It stands at Fő utca 32 near Corvin tér in District I, and the heritage register lists it under the addresses Fő utca 30–32, Corvin János tér 14 and Ponty utca 1–3. It is a protected monument, and the parish says the Capuchin order runs it again.

Hungarian Wikipedia describes a nineteenth-century Romantic historicist exterior mixing Romanesque and Gothic forms. The east façade has a central entrance, a triple window and reliefs of Saint Stephen and Saint Ladislaus, with a stepped gable framed by octagonal pillars and spires. The tower projects forward over the entrance, and a statue of Saint Elizabeth by János Marschalkó, dated 1856, stands above the door.

Inside, the same article describes a nave of four barrel-vaulted bays followed by a narrower choir and an organ by János Garay on the west gallery. The main altar dates from 1760, and its altarpiece dates from 1954. The baroque pews, which the article says came from the Matthias Church in 1876, were restored in 2018 according to the parish.
The former monastery beside the church is a separate property, which Hungarian Wikipedia says has housed a hotel since 2019.
tips: This is a working parish church. Dress and behave as in any place of worship, keep your voice low and avoid photographing during services; check the parish website for service and visiting arrangements.
Look at the two side walls of the nave: the parish says the two façade walls of the Ottoman mosque survive in the present church’s north and south walls.
Do not confuse this church with the nearby Saint Anne church on Batthyány tér; the Capuchin church is on Fő utca by Corvin tér.
The Romantic façade and tower are easiest to appreciate from across the street; a wide lens helps on a narrow pavement.
Chain Bridge and Clark Ádám tér are close to Corvin tér and both have their own pages here, making an easy combined walk.

history.intro: The church grew out of an Ottoman mosque, was baroque in the eighteenth century and was rebuilt in the 1850s in the form seen today.

sections.heading: From mosque to Capuchin church
paragraphs: The parish history says the site was built on in the Middle Ages, probably by the Augustinian friars. The Ottoman-era mosque of Tojgun Pasha is first mentioned in 1555. It had a square plan, a domed roof and a minaret, and a Turkish bath stood nearby. After Buda was retaken in 1686, the Jesuits received the mosque in 1687 and used it as a parish church. In the same year Cardinal György Széchényi, Archbishop of Esztergom, founded the Buda Capuchin monastery.

The Capuchins took possession of the buildings in 1692. In 1697 work began on converting the temporary church under Father Ottó Linzi, and the entrance was moved to the east side. Bishop Lukács Natali consecrated the church to Saint Elizabeth of Hungary on 20 September 1716, and the cloister was completed in 1717.

sections.heading: Baroque additions and the nineteenth-century rebuilding
paragraphs: The parish history records the main altar of 1760, paid for by Countess Erzsébet Bercsényi, and an extension to the east in 1776–1777 with a volute-gabled Baroque façade, possibly by Mátyás Nepauer; the attribution is uncertain. Joseph II restored the church’s parish status in 1787. In 1801 an infant child of Palatine Joseph and Alexandra Pavlovna was buried in the crypt.

The 1849 siege of Buda damaged the church, and in 1854–1856 it was rebuilt under the National Building Directorate in a round-arched style with Gothic Revival elements, led by Ferenc Reitter. Károly Gerster won the construction tender on 20 June 1854 but went bankrupt on 9 January 1856, and Károly Becker completed the work. The rebuilt church was consecrated on 22 November 1856. The heritage register credits the façade to Reitter and Gerster.

sections.heading: War damage and return of the friars
paragraphs: The interior was renovated in 1926–1927 under Ferenc Schömer. In 1944–1945 a bomb destroyed 18th-century altarpieces, the pulpit, stained glass and much of the wall painting, and the interior was restored after the war. The parish says the Capuchin order was dissolved after the war, and Hungarian Wikipedia says the monastery was nationalised in 1950. The exterior was renovated in 1968–1969, and the parish today is again run by the Capuchins.
